text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Russian President Boris Yeltsin says at summit with Chancellor Helmut Kohl that Moscow and NATO will sign charter in Paris.
- Police uncover major operation to dispose illegally of toxic waste, investigate around 40 companies.
- 28,500 company insolvencies expected in Germany in 1997, federal statistics office says.
- Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer calls for conversion rate for European single currency to be announced early.
- First reading of government energy bill runs into opposition.
- Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch expresses confidence in Klaus Zumwinkel, head of Deutsche Post AG, after a call for his resignation from Justice Ministry state secretary.
HANDELSBLATT
- Bundesbank transfers almost nine billion marks to Bonn -- less than in the last few years.
- Ifo institute says business climate in western Germany cooled off in March.
- Volkswagen gives up plan to create its own subsidiary to administer part-time or short-time work.
- Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) want special fund to protect firms from insolvency.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Kohl says Moscow will be given greater international political status.
- Germany will not be supported by UEFA as only European candidate for soccer World Cup in 2006.
- More than 42 billion marks to be invested in German railways between 1998 and 2002, transport ministry says.
- Kohl's coalition plans to change tax reform plans so more tax breaks for farmers remain.
DIE WELT
- Refugees face lower social benefit payments under deal agreed by Kohl's coalition and the SPD.
- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel defends government's policy towards Iran.
- Tietmeyer sticks to hardline on euro, rejecting any relaxation of Maastricht criteria.
- Economic experts doubt whether government's planned tax reform will have significant effect on jobs market.
